title: Double a Number Represented as a Linked List
statement: `head` is a non-empty singly linked list whose nodes each hold one decimal digit; read from `head` to the tail, the digits spell a non-negative integer with its most significant digit first. The number has no leading zeros (the only list that starts with `0` is the single node `0`). Return the head of a list that spells twice that number in the same format.
constraints: The list has between 1 and 10^4 nodes
The number has no leading zeros, except for the number 0 itself
notes:
## Intuition

The usual way to double a number works from the right, carrying into the next digit to the left, but a singly linked list only lets us walk left to right. The brute force copies the digits into an array (or reverses the list) to get around that. There is a neater fact: when you double a digit, the carry it sends left is `1` exactly when the digit is `5` or more, and never more than `1`. So each node can compute its own new digit by looking one step ahead at `node.next.val`, and a single forward pass does the job.

## Approach

1. If the first digit is above `4`, the result gains a digit: put a new `0` node in front of `head`.
2. Walk `node` from `head` to the end.
3. Replace `node.val` with the last digit of twice its value.
4. If the next digit is above `4`, it carries `1` into this node, so add `1`.
5. Return `head` (which may be the new front node).

## Example 1, step by step

`head = [1, 8, 9]`. The first digit `1` is not above 4, so no node is added. At `1`: `2 % 10 = 2`, and the next digit `8 > 4`, so it becomes `3`. At `8`: `16 % 10 = 6`, next digit `9 > 4`, so `7`. At `9`: `18 % 10 = 8`, no next node, so `8`. The list is `[3, 7, 8]`, which is 378 = 2 × 189.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one pass over the list.
- Space: O(1): the list is updated in place, with at most one new node.

## Pitfalls

- The number can have 10^4 digits, so converting it to a regular number overflows; work digit by digit.
- Adding `1` to `(2 × digit) % 10` never makes a second carry, because that value is even and at most `8`.
- Do not forget the extra leading node when the first digit is `5` to `9` (`[5]` becomes `[1, 0]`).

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `head` | first node of the result, possibly a new leading node |
| `node` | the node whose digit is being doubled |
| `node.next.val` | the next digit, which decides the incoming carry |

narration.2: A first digit of 5 or more makes the doubled number one digit longer.
narration.3: So put a 0 node in front; the carry from the old first digit will turn it into a 1.
narration.5: Start walking from the (possibly new) head.
narration.6: Visit every node from the most significant digit to the least.
narration.7: Keep only the units digit of twice this digit.
narration.8: The digit to the right sends a carry of 1 exactly when it is 5 or more.
narration.9: Add that carry; the digit is even and at most 8, so it cannot overflow.
narration.11: Move on to the next digit.
narration.13: Return the head of the doubled number.
